facts.statement: Stethacanthus lived from the Late Devonian to the Late Carboniferous.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Devonian to Late Carboniferous

facts.statement: The genus Stethacanthus was first described by Newberry in 1889.
facts.quote: authority: Newberry, 1889

facts.statement: Fossils of Stethacanthus have been found in Australia, Asia, Europe, and North America.
facts.quote: Fossils have been found in Australia, Asia, Europe and North America.

facts.statement: Stethacanthus was an extinct genus of shark-like cartilaginous fish that died out around 298.9 million years ago.
facts.quote: Stethacanthus is an extinct genus of shark-like cartilaginous fish which lived from the Late Devonian to Late Carboniferous epoch, dying out around 298.9 million years ago.

facts.statement: S. altonensis reached a length of about 1.5 meters, while S. productus reached 3 meters.
facts.quote: S. altonensis had length about 1.5 m, while S. productus reached 3 m.

facts.statement: Small spikes covered the anvil-shaped crest and the shark's head.
facts.quote: Small spikes (enlarged versions of the dermal denticles that commonly cover sharks' skin) covered this crest, and the shark's head as well.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the crest may have been used for mating rituals, clamping onto larger animals, or frightening predators.
facts.quote: The crest may have played a role in mating rituals, aided in clamping to the belly of larger marine animals, or been used to frighten potential predators.

facts.statement: Male Stethacanthus possessed pelvic claspers with non-prismatic calcified cartilage at their distal ends.
facts.quote: In addition to these features, Stethacanthus also had male pelvic claspers with non-prismatic calcified cartilage at the distal ends.

facts.statement: Zangerl hypothesized that the spine-brush complex may have been inflatable, similar to human erectile tissues.
facts.quote: Zangerl asserts that these tubules are similar to erectile tissues in humans, and thus the complex may have been inflatable.

facts.statement: Theories suggest the spine-brush complex and head denticles were used to scare predators by simulating a larger fish's mouth.
facts.quote: The presence of these large denticles has led to theories that the spine-brush complex in combination with the denticles on the head was used to scare away predators by simulating the mouth of a larger fish.

facts.statement: The spine-brush complex is known only in sexually mature males.
facts.quote: The complex has been affirmed only in males, and only in those males that have reached sexual maturity.

facts.statement: It is suggested that the fin whips were used during mating, though their exact purpose is unknown.
facts.quote: The purpose of the fin whips is unknown but it has been suggested that they were used during mating.

facts.statement: Male pelvic claspers were club-shaped at the distal ends and made of non-prismatic globular calcified cartilage.
facts.quote: The males had claspers that were club-shaped at the distal ends and composed of non-prismatic globular calcified cartilage.

facts.statement: Stethacanthus species showed variation in tail shape, ranging from low-angle heterocercal to nearly homocercal.
facts.quote: There was some caudal fin variety among Stethacanthus species; while some had low angle heterocercal tails, some had tails approaching homocercal.

facts.statement: Stethacanthus was a carnivore that likely fed on brachiopods and crinoid ossicles.
facts.quote: It is certain that Stethacanthus was a carnivore, and considering its small size probably fed on brachiopods and crinoid ossicles like other sharks of its time.

facts.statement: Stethacanthus was probably a slow-moving shark due to the drag force produced by its large spine-brush complex.
facts.quote: Therefore, Stethacanthus was probably a slow-moving shark.

facts.statement: Stethacanthus may have been a bottom-dweller based on its small fins and teeth relative to other Paleozoic sharks.
facts.quote: suggesting that Stethacanthus may have been a bottom-dweller.

facts.statement: Stethacanthus may have been migratory, as many specimens were found in the Bear Gulch Limestone, a potential breeding ground.
facts.quote: suggesting that they were migratory.

facts.statement: Species discovered in the late 1800s were initially identified based only on isolated spines, confusing Newberry into thinking they were a new type of fin.
facts.quote: The several species of Stethacanthus discovered in the late 1800s were established based solely upon isolated spines, which initially confused paleontologist John Strong Newberry into thinking the spines constituted a new kind of fin.

facts.statement: The family Stethacanthidae was defined by Richard Lund in 1974 due to the distinct differences of Stethacanthus from other elasmobranchs.
facts.quote: It was not until 1974 that the family Stethacanthidae was defined by Richard Lund because Stethacanthus differed so greatly from other elasmobranchs of the time.

facts.statement: New discoveries have expanded the known range of Stethacanthus to Scotland, Central Russia, and China.
facts.quote: More Stethacanthus specimens have been discovered, expanding their range from the Midwestern United States to the Lower Carboniferous of Bearsden, Scotland and the Lower Tournaisian of the Tula Region of Central Russia and China.

facts.statement: The classification of symmoriids relative to stethacanthids remains a subject of debate.
facts.quote: Relative classifications of symmoriids compared to stethacanthids are still debated.
